units.name: globset
units.role: Compiles glob patterns into matchers and tests candidate paths against single globs or glob sets.
units.description: This unit turns wildcard-style file-matching patterns (like `*.rs`, `!target/`, or `src/**/foo.rs`) into fast, reusable matchers, and checks whether a given file path matches one pattern or a whole collection of patterns at once. It is the shared 'glob matching engine' that other parts of ripgrep rely on to implement .gitignore-style filtering and the --glob/--iglob command-line flags. It must never touch the filesystem, print anything, or make matching decisions about what to search or ignore on its own -- it only compiles patterns and answers 'does this path match', leaving all file-walking and ignore-rule policy to its callers.

units.name: matcher
units.role: Defines the Matcher/Captures trait contract and shared value types (Match, LineTerminator, ByteSet, LineMatchKind) plus $-style replacement interpolation, used by every regex engine and consumer crate in the workspace.
units.description: This unit defines the shared vocabulary that lets ripgrep swap between different text-search engines (the built-in Rust regex engine and the optional PCRE2 engine) without the rest of the program needing to know which one is in use. It specifies what a 'match' is, what a 'capturing group' is, how a line ending is represented, and how to fill in replacement text like $1 or ${name} when a user asks to substitute matched text. It contains no search logic itself and must never talk to the filesystem, network, or any external process -- it only defines shapes and rules that other pieces of the program agree to follow.

units.name: regex-engine
units.role: Default (non-PCRE2) regex compilation and matching engine implementing the shared Matcher trait using regex-automata/regex-syntax.
units.description: This unit is ripgrep's default engine for turning a user's regular expression into something that can be run against file text. It reads the pattern the user typed, applies ripgrep-specific rules such as case-insensitivity, smart case, multi-line mode, word-boundary matching, and 'never match a line terminator', and compiles all of that into a fast, ready-to-run regex using Rust's own regex libraries. It also tries to spot quick 'shortcut' literals inside a pattern so that scanning huge files can go faster. It must never actually read files, talk to the network, or otherwise touch the outside world -- it only turns text patterns into match results over whatever bytes it is handed.

units.name: pcre2-engine
units.role: Adapts the external PCRE2 C library to ripgrep's internal Matcher interface, providing an opt-in alternate regex engine with backreference/lookaround support.
units.description: This unit lets ripgrep understand more powerful pattern syntax, like backreferences and lookaround, that its default, fast search engine cannot express. It does this by handing the pattern off to the well-known PCRE2 C library and translating the results back into ripgrep's own match format. It is only used when a user explicitly opts in (the --pcre2 flag), and it must never be the default engine or silently change matching behavior when the user hasn't asked for it, since calling into external C code is slower and carries different risk than the native engine.

units.name: searcher
units.role: Line-oriented (and multi-line) incremental search engine that drives a Matcher over a byte source and streams matches/context to a caller-provided Sink.
units.description: This is ripgrep's core search engine. Given a pattern-matching object (a Matcher) and a source of bytes (a file, a piece of memory, or anything readable), it reads through the data piece by piece, finds the lines that match, keeps track of line numbers, gathers the lines of context around a match, and detects whether the data looks like binary (non-text) content so it can stop early. It hands every match and context line it finds to a caller-supplied receiver (a Sink) rather than printing anything itself. It must never decide how results are displayed or colored, and it must never depend on any specific pattern-matching implementation -- it only depends on the generic Matcher contract.

units.name: printer
units.role: Formats and writes search results (from the searcher unit, driven by the matcher unit) into human- or machine-readable output streams.
units.description: This unit takes the raw matches that the search engine finds inside files and turns them into something a person or another program can actually read. It offers three output styles: a classic grep-style text listing (with line numbers, colored highlights, context lines, optional search-and-replace text, and clickable file links for terminals that support it), a JSON-lines stream for tools to consume, and a summary/count view that just reports how many matches or files matched. It also tallies statistics like elapsed time, bytes searched, and match counts. This unit must never decide what to search for or how to search a file -- it only formats and writes out results it is given.

units.name: cli-support
units.role: OS/terminal-facing plumbing layer providing subprocess-backed readers, byte escaping, pattern-file ingestion, hostname lookup, size parsing, and buffered/colored stdout writers for the ripgrep CLI.
units.description: This is a toolbox of small operating-system helpers used by the ripgrep command-line program. It knows how to launch an external program (like gzip or a custom filter script) and read its output as if it were a file, so ripgrep can search inside compressed or otherwise transformed files; it knows how to safely display bytes that aren't normal printable text in error messages and terminal output; it can read the list of search patterns from a file or from piped-in input; it can look up the computer's network name; it can turn sizes like '2M' into a byte count; and it decides whether to print results to the screen quickly or efficiently, with or without color. It must never try to interpret or evaluate what is being searched for or found -- it only shuttles bytes between the outside world and the rest of the program.

units.name: index
units.role: Standalone, feature-gated crate that builds and opens an on-disk ngram index database and provides (currently unwired) machinery for turning a regex into a query over that index.
units.description: This is an experimental, opt-in add-on for ripgrep that tries to speed up repeated searches over the same set of files by building a small local database ahead of time. It works by chopping the text of files into short overlapping fragments and recording which fragments appear in which files, plus turning a search pattern into a query over those fragments, so that later a search could skip files that provably cannot contain a match without having to open and read them. It must never be relied upon to definitively confirm a match, and it must never silently replace ripgrep's real read-the-file search -- it is disabled by default and gated behind the `unstable-index` feature specifically because it is unfinished and not production quality.

units.name: ignore-walk
units.role: Recursive, gitignore-aware directory traversal engine that filters and yields candidate file paths for searching, sequentially or in parallel.
units.description: This unit decides which files and folders ripgrep should even look at before any text searching happens. It walks a directory tree (optionally spreading the work across several worker threads for speed), and at every step it checks the file or folder name against the rules people expect from Git: .gitignore files, a global git-excludes file, .git/info/exclude, hidden-file conventions, and any command-line overrides like --glob or --type rust. It hands back a stream of 'these paths are worth searching' entries (or errors, if a directory couldn't be read). It must never itself read the contents of the files it finds, run the search, or decide what counts as a match -- its job stops at deciding which paths exist and are eligible to be searched.

units.name: flags
units.role: Parses CLI arguments and config-file settings into a validated configuration object (HiArgs) that the rest of the rg binary uses to build its matcher/printer/walker, and generates --help, man-page, and shell-completion text from the same flag definitions.
units.description: This is ripgrep's command-line rulebook. It defines every flag and switch the tool understands (like -i for case-insensitive search, or --json for machine-readable output), reads any saved defaults from a config file, and turns whatever the user actually typed into one fully checked, ready-to-use plan of action that the rest of the program executes. It also reuses that same rulebook to automatically generate the --help text, the man page, and the shell auto-complete scripts, so the documentation can never drift out of sync with the real flags. It must never actually perform a search, print search results, or walk the filesystem for matches itself -- its job stops at producing a validated plan (or a help/version/completion string) and handing it off.

units.name: app
units.role: Top-level process orchestration for the rg binary: consumes parsed configuration, drives directory walking + searching + printing + stats, and owns process exit codes, logging, and ripgrep's own error/warning message formatting.
units.description: This is the steering wheel and dashboard of the ripgrep command-line tool. Once the program's settings have been read and understood (by the flags unit), this unit is what actually runs the show: it walks through files and directories, hands each file to the searching machinery, prints results and summary statistics to the screen, and decides what exit code the program ends with. It also owns ripgrep's own way of printing warnings and error lines (prefixed with 'rg:'), its simple debug logger, and the notion of a 'thing to search' (a file, or standard input). It must never itself decide how a regex matches text, how ignore files are parsed, or how results are colored/formatted -- it only wires those pieces together and drives them.

violations_observed.location: crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs (imports crate::haystack::{Haystack, HaystackBuilder} and crate::search::{PatternMatcher, Printer, SearchWorker, SearchWorkerBuilder})
violations_observed.note: Not a boundary violation in the strict sense -- every item flags uses is a declared pub(crate) entrypoint of app -- but it creates a genuine dependency cycle: app::main calls flags::parse()/HiArgs (flags -> consumed by app), while HiArgs's own methods construct and return app's SearchWorker/Haystack types (app's vocabulary -> reused by flags). This means 'flags' and 'app' are not cleanly layered; they co-evolve as one argument-resolution/orchestration subsystem split across two files for readability rather than two independently substitutable units. A stricter decomposition might merge them into a single unit, at the cost of a much larger single unit for the CLI's argument-to-execution pipeline.
